title: Traffic death rates run highest where the fewest people live
dek: About 41,000 people a year died in U.S. traffic crashes from 2020 to 2024. Per resident, the toll is several times higher in thinly settled counties than in big cities, and serious injuries, which are far more common, have no national county map at all.
author: Drafted by Claude for Robbie King
caption: Average yearly traffic deaths per 100,000 residents, 2020–2024, by county (NHTSA FARS). Darker purple means a higher rate; each shade holds a fifth of counties, and the darkest starts at 30.7. Deaths are counted where the crash happened. Connecticut is blank because its crash records use the old county codes.
method: Every number from Mapwich data in the text was computed from Mapwich's exported state and county values with a script kept in the repository (`apps/web/scripts/specials-numbers/traffic-deaths.mjs`); the chart and table are computed from the same files when the site is built. Mapwich stores rates, not counts. Death counts in the text are rebuilt from the rates the same way the rates were made: rate × residents ÷ 100,000, with residents from the ACS 2020–2024 population (2015–2019 for years before 2020). National figures are rebuilt from state values, so they can differ by a few dozen deaths from NHTSA's published totals. Deaths per mile driven divide 2020–2024 average deaths by 2024 vehicle miles on counted roads (FHWA HPMS), which leave out some local roads, so they run higher than NHTSA's national figures. Statements that one measure "tends to" rise with another rest on Spearman rank correlations (density and death rate: −0.52 nationally, −0.59 within states, which removes each state's average rank first; miles per resident and density: −0.46; miles per resident and death rate: 0.50; share of Native residents and death rate: 0.08). Outside figures: NHTSA, [*Overview of Motor Vehicle Traffic Crashes in 2023*](https://crashstats.nhtsa.dot.gov/Api/Public/ViewPublication/813705) (DOT HS 813 705) and [*Rural/Urban Comparison of Traffic Fatalities: 2022 Data*](https://crashstats.nhtsa.dot.gov/Api/Public/ViewPublication/813599) (DOT HS 813 599); FHWA, [*National Performance Management Measures: Highway Safety Improvement Program*](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2016/03/15/2016-05202/national-performance-management-measures-highway-safety-improvement-program), 81 FR 13882 (2016); [CDC, Tribal Road Safety](https://www.cdc.gov/tribal-road-safety/about/index.html); [National Park Service, Fort Wingate Historic District](https://www.nps.gov/places/fort-wingate-historic-district.htm); U.S. Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, [*Enhancing Tribal Self-Governance and Safety of Indian Roads*](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-116shrg36243/html/CHRG-116shrg36243.htm), S. Hrg. 116-15 (2019); [University of Arizona, Native American Advancement, Initiatives and Research: Navajo Nation](https://naair.arizona.edu/navajo-nation). This piece was drafted by Claude, an AI model, from Mapwich data, and reviewed by Robbie King before publication.

body.html:
From 2020 through 2024, about 41,000 people a year died in motor vehicle crashes in the United States: 12.3 for every 100,000 residents, according to NHTSA's Fatality Analysis Reporting System. The map above shows where those crashes happened, county by county.

By state, Mississippi has the highest rate, 25.1 deaths per 100,000 residents a year, followed by Wyoming (21.4), Arkansas (20.9), New Mexico (20.7) and South Carolina (20.6). Massachusetts has the lowest, 5.4, with Rhode Island, New York, the District of Columbia and Hawaii close behind. Mississippi's rate is 4.7 times Massachusetts's.

A rise, then a slow fall

Deaths jumped during the pandemic. The national rate went from 11.2 per 100,000 in 2019 to 12.9 in 2021, when about 43,200 people died, the highest single year from 2014-2024. It has fallen every year since, to 11.7 in 2024, but that is still higher than any year from 2015 to 2019.

Year Traffic deaths per 100,000 residents
2015 10.9
2016 11.6
2017 11.5
2018 11.3
2019 11.2
2020 11.6
2021 12.9
2022 12.8
2023 12.2
2024 11.7

National rate for each year, from NHTSA's FARS files. 2015–2019 use the 2015–2019 ACS population; 2020–2024 use the 2020–2024 population.

Fewer people, higher rates

The clearest pattern on the map is density. Sort the 3,135 counties with a value by people per square mile and cut them into ten equal groups. In the least crowded tenth, under 4 people per square mile, the typical county's rate is 34.9. In the most crowded tenth, 427 people per square mile and up, it is 8.4, about a quarter as high.

body.title: Traffic death rates fall as counties get more crowded
body.caption: Median county traffic death rate (2020–2024 yearly average, NHTSA FARS) in each tenth of counties, sorted by people per square mile (ACS 2020–2024). Medians, because a few tiny counties have extreme rates.

body.html:
It isn't just rural states against urban ones. Inside each state, the emptier counties still tend to have the higher death rates, and the pattern is a little stronger within states than across the country as a whole. Counties with fewer than 50 people per square mile hold 8.8% of the people but 17.3% of the deaths, a combined rate of 24.1. Counties with 500 or more hold 54.2% of the people and 39.1% of the deaths, a combined rate of 8.9.

Driving goes along with it. People in emptier counties tend to drive more, and counties with more driving per resident tend to have higher death rates. Per mile driven, though, the gap narrows but doesn't close. Dividing deaths by miles driven on counted roads gives 1.73 deaths per 100 million vehicle miles in the least crowded tenth of counties and 1.16 in the most crowded. NHTSA's own figures for 2022 show a similar gap: 1.68 deaths per 100 million miles in rural areas and 1.15 in urban ones. Rural areas held about 20% of the population and 41% of the deaths, and about two-thirds of rural deaths were in crashes where a vehicle left its lane or the road.

Counted where the crash happens

The rate on this map divides deaths where crashes happened by the people who live there. Where few people live and many drive through, the rate can soar. West Texas shows it most clearly.

body.caption: West Texas, by county. Same colors as the main map. Of the 27 Texas counties west of 101°W and south of 33°N, 23 are in the darkest shade. The four exceptions, El Paso, Midland, Ector and Val Verde, are the area's four most populous counties.

body.html:
Loving County, Texas, had 64 residents in the 2020 Census, and the ACS estimate is 33. Nineteen people died in crashes there over the five years, so its rate is 11,520 per 100,000, by far the highest in the country. Its counted roads carry 7,113 vehicle miles a day for every resident, 236 times the typical county. Hudspeth and Culberson counties, east of El Paso, had 71 deaths between them and about 5,600 residents. Their rates, 258.6 and 246.0, say as much about the traffic passing through as about the people who live there.

Small numbers matter too. In a county of 2,000 people, one more death in five years moves the yearly rate by 10. Of the 46 counties with rates above 100, 44 have fewer than 10,000 residents. And 31 counties had no traffic deaths at all from 2020 to 2024.

body.title: Seven counties, from nearly empty to very crowded
body.caption: Vehicle miles per resident: daily miles driven on counted roads in the county, per resident (FHWA HPMS 2024). Shelby County, Tennessee, home to Memphis, is a reminder that density isn't everything.

body.html:
Shelby County's rate, 26.6, is 2.2 times the national rate, the ninth-highest of the 607 counties with 100,000 or more residents. New York County (Manhattan), at 2.3, and Arlington County, Virginia, at 2.2, have the lowest.

The Four Corners

A second cluster stands out in the Southwest, and through-traffic doesn't explain it the same way.

body.caption: The Four Corners, by county. Same colors as the main map. Apache, Navajo and Coconino counties in Arizona, McKinley and Cibola in New Mexico, and San Juan County, Utah, are all in the darkest shade.

body.html:
Apache, Navajo and Coconino counties in Arizona and McKinley County in New Mexico each have rates between 36.9 and 38.6, roughly twice their states' rates (Arizona 16.5, New Mexico 20.7). Together they recorded 730 deaths in five years. Their vehicle miles per resident, 35 to 47 a day, are only modestly above the typical county's 30. Much of the Navajo Nation, the largest reservation in the United States, lies in these counties; in Apache and McKinley counties, 71% and 75% of residents are American Indian (ACS 2020–2024).

Nationally, counties with more Native residents don't consistently have higher death rates, partly because the 12 Alaska counties where Native residents are a quarter or more of the population have low rates (median 5.9). Outside Alaska, the 35 such counties have a combined rate of 37.3, about three times the national rate.

The CDC reports that American Indian and Alaska Native people have the highest motor vehicle death rates of any racial or ethnic group. The roads they travel have a history. In the 1860s the U.S. Army forced thousands of Navajo people on a 400-mile march, the Long Walk, to the Bosque Redondo Reservation in New Mexico; a treaty in 1868 let them return home. Today the Bureau of Indian Affairs runs a road system on tribal lands. At a 2019 Senate hearing, it said about 17,130 miles of those roads were unimproved earth roads, with $392 million in deferred maintenance in 2018. The Federal Highway Administration told the same hearing that "many Tribes are not adequately represented in State and national crash databases," so counts like these may be low.

Serious injuries: the map we don't have

For every traffic death there are many more serious injuries, but there is no national county map of them, and Mapwich doesn't have one. FARS, the source of the death counts, covers fatal crashes only. NHTSA estimates injuries from a sample of police crash reports: about 2.44 million people were injured in 2023, about 60 for every death. Those are national estimates, not county ones, and they count injuries of every severity.

Serious injuries are counted by the states. A 2016 federal rule requires every state transportation department to track the number of serious injuries, using a common definition taken from police crash reports, and to set targets on five-year averages. Those counts sit in each state's own crash records, and Mapwich hasn't brought them together.

What the map can't tell us

This map counts deaths where crashes happened, not where the people who died resided. It can't say who was driving, how fast, or why a crash happened, and it can't separate the road from the traffic on it. A county's rate can also swing on a handful of crashes.

What it does show is steady. Traffic deaths per resident are highest in the emptiest counties, and the gap holds within states and per mile driven. In a few places the numbers mostly reflect traffic passing through. In others, like the Navajo Nation, they fall on the people who live there.

title: Work from home, work out more? What the county map can and can't tell us
dek: Counties where more people work from home have fewer adults who skip exercise altogether. The pattern is strong and it's real, but most of it follows income and education, and part of it is built into how the health numbers are made.
author: Drafted by Claude for Robbie King
caption: Work from home (2020–2024) against adults with no leisure-time exercise (2023), by county. Blue counties have many home workers and few non-exercisers; gold counties the reverse. 2,956 counties have both values; Kentucky and Pennsylvania are blank because the inactivity data has no county values for them.
method: Every number from Mapwich data in the text was computed from Mapwich's exported county values with a script kept in the repository (`apps/web/scripts/specials-numbers/work-from-home-and-exercise.mjs`); the chart and tables are computed from the same files when the site is built. Correlations are Spearman rank correlations (ρ). "Within states" removes each state's average rank first. "Holding income and education equal" is a partial rank correlation: both measures' ranks are adjusted for the ranks of median household income and the bachelor's degree share before they are compared. Virginia's independent cities count as counties, as the Census Bureau treats them. The inactivity estimates come from a statistical model ([CDC PLACES methodology](https://www.cdc.gov/places/methodology/index.html)); the survey question is on [CDC's measure definitions page](https://www.cdc.gov/places/measure-definitions/health-risk-behaviors.html). The history of Pine Ridge and Rosebud draws on [Oglala Lakota County](https://oglalalakotacountysd.gov/about-3/), the [Bureau of Indian Affairs](https://www.bia.gov/regional-offices/great-plains/south-dakota/rosebud-agency), [*United States v. Sioux Nation of Indians*, 448 U.S. 371 (1980)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/448/371) and the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, [*Broken Promises: Continuing Federal Funding Shortfall for Native Americans*](https://www.usccr.gov/reports/2018/broken-promises-continuing-federal-funding-shortfall-native-americans) (2018). This piece was drafted by Claude, an AI model, from Mapwich data, and checked against that data before publication.

body.html:
Look at the map above and two colors do most of the talking. Blue marks counties in the top third for the share of workers who work from home and the bottom third for adults who got no exercise at all in the past month. Gold marks the opposite: few home workers, many adults with no leisure-time activity. Blue is common in the West: 43 of Colorado's 64 counties are blue, and 29 of Washington's 39. About half of the 632 blue counties have 100 or more people per square mile. Gold is concentrated in the South. In Mississippi, 67 of 82 counties are gold, and 483 of the 596 gold counties nationwide are in 14 southern states from Texas to Virginia.

Across the 2,956 counties with both numbers, the link is strong: a rank correlation of −0.62. It is not just one region of the country against another, either. Comparing counties only with others in the same state, it is still −0.53.

So does working from home get people moving? The tempting story writes itself: no commute, more time for a walk. The county data can't confirm that story, and when you look closely, most of the pattern turns out to be about something else.

How big the gap is

Sort the counties by their work-from-home share and cut them into ten equal groups of about 296 counties each. In the tenth with the fewest home workers (under 4.2% of workers), an average of 33.1% of adults report no leisure-time exercise. In the tenth with the most (16.4% and up), it's 20.8%.

body.title: Fewer adults skip exercise in counties where more people work from home
body.caption: Work from home is the share of workers 16 and over who usually worked from home (ACS 2020–2024). No leisure-time exercise is the age-adjusted share of adults who answered no to any exercise outside their job in the past month (CDC PLACES, 2023).

body.html:
That's a gap of about 12 percentage points, in a measure where the typical county sits at 26.5%. It's a big difference, but it doesn't tell us why.

Virginia, where the two line up

Virginia shows the pattern clearly. Across its 133 counties and independent cities the rank correlation is −0.72, stronger than the national figure. The close-up below runs from the Washington suburbs in the northeast to the rural counties of the southwest.

body.caption: Virginia and West Virginia, by county. Northern Virginia, at top right, is mostly blue: seven of its nine counties and independent cities. West Virginia, at left, is mostly gold, brown or dark: 47 of its 55 counties are in the top third for inactivity. Same colors as the main map.

body.html:
In Arlington County, 35.3% of workers work from home and 15.1% of adults report no leisure-time exercise. In Giles County, in the southwest, 2.5% work from home and 24.9% report no exercise. Grayson County, also in the southwest, is at 5.2% and 31.3%.

The table shows how else these counties differ.

body.title: Four counties in northern and central Virginia, four in the southwest
body.caption: Median household income and the share of adults 25 and over with a bachelor's degree are ACS 2020–2024 estimates.

body.html:
In the first four, median household incomes run from $104,400 to $181,800, and three in five adults or more have a bachelor's degree. In the four southwestern counties incomes are between $47,730 and $65,690 and fewer than one adult in five has a degree. Working from home, exercise, income and education all move together here. Any one of them could be standing in for the others.

The northern Plains, where the pattern breaks

Now move to the Dakotas and eastern Montana. Here the link mostly disappears: within South Dakota the correlation is 0.03, essentially none; in North Dakota −0.14; in Montana −0.09.

body.caption: The Dakotas and eastern Montana, by county. Much of the region is blue or pale, but five South Dakota counties are dark: in the top third for both working from home and inactivity. Same colors as the main map.

body.html:
Some of the highest work-from-home shares in the country are here, in places with very few people. Perkins County, South Dakota, about one person per square mile, has a work-from-home share of 32.9%, sixth-highest of the 2,956 counties and above Fairfax County's 28.7%. Yet its inactivity rate, 23.6%, is unremarkable. Kidder County, North Dakota, is similar: 22.1% working from home, 24.1% inactive.

These numbers likely mean something different from home office work in a suburb. The data here can't say what Perkins County's home workers do, but Census Bureau research has long found self-employed workers overrepresented among home-based workers, and in the 1960s most were family farmers and professionals. The exercise question matters too. It asks about activity "other than your regular job." Someone who works hard all day outdoors can answer no. Across the 417 counties nationwide with fewer than six people per square mile, the correlation is −0.33, about half the national figure.

In the region, inactivity follows income far more closely than working from home. Within South Dakota, the correlation between median household income and inactivity is −0.78. The two South Dakota counties with the highest inactivity rates, Todd (42.3%) and Oglala Lakota (41.7%), have median household incomes near $42,000 and work-from-home shares under 4%.

Oglala Lakota County lies entirely within the Pine Ridge Reservation, and Todd County within the Rosebud Sioux Reservation. Their low incomes and poor health have a much stronger explanation than anything about work: generations of U.S. policy toward Native nations. The Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868 set the Black Hills apart for the Sioux; in 1877 Congress took them without the consent of three-fourths of adult men that the treaty required, a taking the Supreme Court ruled in 1980 must be paid for, with interest. In exchange for the "forced dispossession" of Native land and the removal of tribes from their homelands, the government promised services, but the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights found in 2018 that those programs "remain chronically underfunded": in 2016 the Indian Health Service spent $2,834 per person, against $9,990 per person in federal health spending nationwide.

It's older than the pandemic

If remote office work caused the pattern, you'd expect it to be weak before 2020. It wasn't. Using the 2015–2019 work-from-home shares, when the typical county had 4.5% of workers at home (against 8.7% in 2020–2024), the correlation with the 2023 inactivity estimates is already −0.51. With 2010–2014 shares it's −0.49. The places where people work from home have long been different kinds of places.

Income, education and a model

Several other county measures line up with inactivity at least as strongly as working from home does, and they line up with working from home, too.

body.title: What else lines up with skipping exercise
body.caption: Income per person, household income and the bachelor's degree share each line up with inactivity more closely than working from home does, and each rises with working from home too. Population density and median age barely line up with inactivity.

body.html:
When we hold income and education equal, comparing counties that rank alike on median household income and the bachelor's degree share, the link between working from home and inactivity shrinks from −0.62 to −0.22. Adding population density and median age brings it to −0.16. Within groups of counties at similar income levels it is between −0.36 and −0.56. Something is left, but most of the pattern is about who lives in a county, not how they get to work.

Age is a small factor partly by design: the inactivity rates are age-adjusted, so a county with many retirees is not marked down for it.

There's one more reason to be careful. The inactivity numbers aren't a direct count. CDC's PLACES project estimates them with a statistical model: it takes national survey answers and predicts each county's rate using its residents' age, sex, race and ethnicity, and education, plus the share of the county's adults living below 150% of the poverty line, from the same Census survey that measures working from home (CDC PLACES methodology). So education and poverty are two of the model's inputs, and they are also two of the strongest companions of working from home. Part of the correlation is built in by the way the estimates are made. That does not make the pattern false, but the county estimates may line up with education and poverty more neatly than the true rates do.

One more thing we couldn't test: the mix of jobs. Some jobs can be done from home and many can't. If the ones that can are concentrated in the same counties as college graduates and higher incomes, that alone would produce much of this pattern. Mapwich doesn't have county occupation data yet, so we can't separate the job from the person doing it.

What the map can't tell us

None of this shows that working from home makes anyone more active, or less. A correlation across counties is a statement about places, not people. The home workers in Arlington and the non-exercisers in Grayson County may not be the same people at all. Answering the real question would take data that follows individuals: how they work, and how they spend the time they don't spend commuting.

What the map does show is useful on its own. Places where working from home is common tend to be places where more adults stay active, and both tend to be places with more money and more college degrees. Where that bundle comes apart, as on the northern Plains, the work-from-home number stops predicting much at all.
